topic: Anne Treisman (1960/1964): Attenuation Theory — Why Your Ignored Ear Suddenly Hijacks Your Mouth When the Story Jumps Ears!
visual_mode_reason: 24-year-old Oxford graduate student Anne Treisman's brilliant 1960/1964 dichotic story-swap experiment — proving unattended speech isn't 'switched to zero' (Broadbent) but *turned down like a dimmer knob (attenuated)* so your own name or a meaningful sentence continuation ('I SAW THE GIRL... song was wishing / JUMPING') leaps across ears right into your mouth — bridges classic attention psychology to cortical gain & semantic priming.

primary_case.title: Anne M. Treisman's 1960/1964 Oxford Dichotic Channel-Swap & 'Attenuation Theory' of Selective Attention
primary_case.place: Institute of Experimental Psychology, University of Oxford

people.name: Anne Marie Treisman
people.role: 24-year-old Oxford doctoral student (National Medal of Science laureate presented by President Obama!) who overturned her own mentor group's 'All-or-Nothing Filter' with one ingenious mid-sentence ear swap.

people.name: Donald E. Broadbent & J. Anthony Deutsch
people.role: Rival architects of strict 'Early Selection' (1958, filter blocks ALL meaning) vs 'Late Selection' (1963, brain decodes 100% of every voice's meaning!) — both reconciled by Treisman's smart 'Dimmer Knob' middle ground.

core_facts.fact: By 1959, attention psychology was split by a paradox: Colin Cherry & **Donald Broadbent (1958)** claimed an early mechanical switch **blocks 100% of unattended meaning** — yet why do you whip your head around across a noisy party the instant someone whispers **YOUR OWN NAME**, *'Fire!'*, or your child's cry?.

At age 24 at Oxford (1960 *Quarterly Journal*; **1964 *JVLVB* & *British Medical Bulletin***, SRC1, SRC2), **Anne Treisman** designed a delightfully sneaky dichotic shadowing test: Volunteers shadowed the **Right Ear** strictly (*'Repeat ONLY the right ear, ignore the left ear completely!'*) while hearing coherent prose (*'Sitting at a mahogany table with her head in her hands...'*).

Right in the middle of a sentence, **Treisman silently swapped the two stories between headphone ears**: suddenly the Right Ear began spouting random nonsense words, while the meaningful continuation of the sentence jumped into the **'ignored' Left Ear**.

If Broadbent's '100% OFF switch' were true, volunteers would never notice the Left Ear. Instead, **volunteers spontaneously blurred right across to the 'ignored' Left Ear for 1 to 2 words** (saying the meaningful word from the WRONG ear aloud!) before snapping back to the Right Ear — and most didn't even realize their mouth had briefly hopped ears.

In **1964 (SRC1)**, Treisman tested bilinguals (English-French), identical voices in two languages, and poetry vs technical prose: when an **attended English story met an unattended French translation of the EXACT SAME story** slightly offset in time, bilinguals frequently **recognized that both ears carried the same meaning** — proving attenuated signals still nudge deep semantic dictionary entries.

From these gems, Treisman unveiled **Attenuation Theory**: the early attention filter is **NOT an ON/OFF light switch — it is a VOLUME DIMMER KNOB (Attenuator)**. Attended speech enters at **100% signal strength**; unattended speech is **turned down (attenuated)** to a quiet trickle rather than erased to zero.

Inside your mental dictionary, each word has its own **activation threshold**: permanently VIP alarms (**your own name, 'Help!', 'Fire!'**) have **permanently hair-trigger low thresholds**, AND preceding sentence context (*'I ate peanut butter and...'*) temporarily lowers the threshold for *'jelly'* — so even an **attenuated trickle** from the ignored ear pushes *'jelly'* or *'[Your Name]'* right over threshold into conscious awareness.

When rivals Deutsch & Deutsch (1963) swung to the opposite extreme claiming *everything* is 100% analyzed ('Late Selection'), **Treisman & Geffen (1967, SRC3)** crushed that myth too: asking listeners to tap a ruler whenever a target word appeared yielded **86.5% hits in the attended ear vs just 8.7% in the unattended ear** — proving the dimmer knob really DOES turn unattended speech way down without shutting it to 0.0%.

Three decades (30 years) after Treisman's 1960–1964 attenuation model, human magnetoencephalography and auditory-cortex ERP studies confirmed graded gain modulation rather than complete peripheral channel shutoff.

wow_facts.fact: Tell a student *'Repeat ONLY the right ear!'* — then mid-sentence swap the coherent story into the ignored left ear: **their own mouth blurts out the next word from the 'ignored' left ear** before catching itself.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Meaning pulled their voice right across a headphone boundary they swore they weren't listening to.

wow_facts.fact: Play a story in English to a bilingual's right ear and the **French translation** of that exact story quietly into their left ear (Treisman 1964): even though Cherry proved strangers miss German in the left ear, bilinguals suddenly say ***'Hey — the French guy on my left is telling the exact same story!'***
wow_facts.why_surprising: Primed meaning hears through language disguises.

wow_facts.fact: Why did Broadbent think the filter was 0% and Deutsch think it was 100%? **Treisman & Geffen (1967)** measured the exact number with a ruler tap: **86.5% attended vs 8.7% unattended** — not zero, not a hundred, an **attenuated dimmer knob**.
wow_facts.why_surprising: One elegant number settled psychology's biggest war.

wow_facts.fact: Why do you hear your baby whimper or a coworker whisper your name across a roaring airport lounge while missing 50 louder conversations closer to your chair? **Hair-trigger dictionary thresholds + Treisman's dimmer knob!**
wow_facts.why_surprising: Evolution kept critical survival alarms on hair-trigger sensitivity.

misconceptions.myth: Unattended sounds are 100% deleted at the eardrum before reaching word meaning ('strict early block').
misconceptions.truth: Treisman proved unattended speech is *attenuated*, not deleted — high-priority personal words (your name) and context-primed words still cross dictionary thresholds (~8.7% breakthrough rate).

misconceptions.myth: Your subconscious brain secretly understands 100% of every conversation in a crowded room ('pure late selection').
misconceptions.truth: Treisman & Geffen's 86.5% vs 8.7% target-tapping test proved 91% of ordinary un-primed words in an ignored stream fail to cross lexical awareness.

misconceptions.myth: Hearing your own name across a room means you have 'super-hearing'.
misconceptions.truth: Your ears didn't get louder — your lifetime mental dictionary entry for your own name sits permanently inches below the firing line so even a 10% attenuated whisper trips it.

everyday_hooks: Hearing your own first name — or the exact project code you've been stressing over all week! — pop out crystal-clear from three tables away in a noisy coffee shop.
Overhearing a half-whispered sentence when you already know the topic ('primed low threshold') versus hearing mush when you lack context.

Understanding why emergency hospital/aviation alerts lead with a person's **name or call-sign FIRST** before the critical instruction — tripping the low-threshold door open so the rest of the sentence gets full 100% gain.
